content: A factory that has to constantly change its processes and materials to meet dozens of different customer-specific requirements will have lower efficiency and higher costs than a factory that produces a standardized product line in high volume. Critics of this approach would argue that Aiguille should focus on complying with the most common international standards (ASTM, ISO) and producing a standardized, high-quality product line. This is the price of admission. The prices of key industrial metals (iron ore, copper, nickel) and precious metals (gold, platinum) are a direct proxy for the financial health and investment appetite of mining companies. A sustained period of high copper prices, for example, will incentivize mining companies to expand existing operations and invest in new projects ("greenfield" and "brownfield" expansions). Aiguille must therefore closely monitor commodity price trends and forecasts from sources like the London Metal Exchange (LME), financial news outlets like Bloomberg and Reuters, and the quarterly reports of the mining majors themselves. These reports often contain explicit guidance on planned capital expenditures (CapEx) and production volumes for the upcoming year, which are direct inputs for demand forecasting. Industry-specific publications, trade association reports, and market research studies are another treasure trove of demand indicators. There is also the risk of misinterpreting a signal or acting on a false positive, leading to costly mistakes, such as building up inventory for a demand surge that never materializes. The argument is that the complexity and uncertainty of interpreting these signals outweigh their potential benefits. For example, a KIT could be "Demand for GET in the Australian Iron Ore Sector." The key indicators would be the price of iron ore, the announced CapEx of BHP, Rio Tinto, and Fortescue Metals Group, and reports from the Australian Bureau of Statistics on mining investment. This focused approach reduces the noise and makes the analysis manageable. A decision to increase production would only be made if, for example, commodity prices are up, a major customer has announced an expansion, and a leading market research firm has upgraded its forecast for the sector. This triangulation of evidence provides a much higher degree of confidence.
